papers.title: stEDGE enables edge-guided multiscale reconstruction of hierarchical spatial domains and transition interfaces in spatial transcriptomics
papers.summary: stEDGE is a computational method for analyzing spatial transcriptomics data that uses edge information to reconstruct spatial domains at multiple scales, from broad tissue regions down to finer substructures. It also identifies transition interfaces, the boundary zones between different spatial domains, which are often biologically important but hard to detect. The tool aims to provide a more hierarchical and precise map of tissue organization compared to standard clustering-based spatial domain detection methods.
papers.why: Precise identification of spatial domains and their transition interfaces could help map perineuronal net boundaries and interneuron subregions in spatial transcriptomics data, refining how autophagy/mitophagy signatures are localized relative to microenvironmental niches.

papers.title: Image-guided alignment of consecutive multi-modal tissue slides.
papers.summary: This paper describes a method for aligning consecutive tissue sections that were processed with different imaging or omics modalities, using image features to guide the registration. Such alignment is crucial when combining data types like spatial transcriptomics and spatial metabolomics, which are typically measured on separate but adjacent slides. The abstract itself is minimal, suggesting the full text likely details the algorithm, validation, and performance metrics.
papers.why: Accurately co-registering consecutive slides is essential for integrating spatial transcriptomics and spatial metabolomics data in the same tissue region, directly supporting multi-modal analysis of interneurons and perineuronal nets.

papers.title: Cinchonain Ib alleviates the cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury by regulating mitophagy through AKT/mTOR signaling pathway.
papers.summary: This study investigates Cinchonain Ib, a natural compound, as a potential treatment for brain damage caused by stroke-like ischemia-reperfusion injury. The researchers found that this compound helps protect neurons by regulating mitophagy, the process by which cells clear out damaged mitochondria. The protective effect works through the AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, a well-known cellular pathway that controls cell survival and autophagy.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it demonstrates pharmacological modulation of mitophagy via AKT/mTOR signaling in a neuronal injury context, directly relating to the project's core focus on mitophagy regulation mechanisms in the brain.

papers.title: Autophagy in hypothalamic POMC and AgRP neurons: mechanisms and therapeutic implications for obesity.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how autophagy, the cell's process for recycling damaged components, operates in two key types of hypothalamic neurons (POMC and AgRP) that control hunger and energy balance. It discusses the molecular mechanisms linking autophagy dysfunction in these neurons to obesity development. The paper also explores potential therapeutic strategies that target autophagy pathways to treat obesity.
papers.why: This work is relevant because it addresses autophagy mechanisms in specific neuronal subtypes, offering conceptual and mechanistic parallels that could inform your studies of mitophagy/autophagy in interneurons, even though the brain region and neuron types differ from your primary focus.

papers.title: NAD<sup>+</sup>-sirtuin-mitochondrial quality control in lens epithelial cells: a candidate modulatory network in crystalline lens aging.
papers.summary: This paper proposes that a network involving NAD+, sirtuins, and mitochondrial quality control mechanisms plays a role in the aging of lens epithelial cells in the eye. It suggests that declining NAD+ levels and impaired sirtuin activity may lead to reduced mitochondrial quality control, contributing to lens aging and potentially cataract formation. The work is largely conceptual/review-like, framing this molecular network as a candidate target for future study.
papers.why: Although focused on lens tissue rather than brain, this paper is relevant because it reinforces the broader mechanistic link between NAD+-sirtuin signaling and mitochondrial quality control (mitophagy), a pathway central to neuronal mitophagy research.

papers.title: Mitophagy-driven immune evasion in skin cancer: multidimensional regulatory networks and context-dependent therapeutic strategies—a narrative review
papers.summary: This narrative review discusses how mitophagy, the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria, contributes to immune evasion in skin cancer. It outlines the regulatory networks connecting mitophagy pathways to tumor immune escape mechanisms. The paper also proposes context-dependent therapeutic strategies that target mitophagy to improve anti-tumor immunity.
papers.why: While focused on skin cancer rather than neurons, this review's detailed mechanistic breakdown of mitophagy regulatory pathways could offer transferable molecular insights relevant to studying mitophagy in neuronal contexts.

papers.title: Mitophagy in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: from molecular mechanisms to therapeutic opportunities.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how mitophagy, the process cells use to clear damaged mitochondria, becomes dysregulated in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a scarring lung disease. It covers the molecular pathways involved, such as PINK1/Parkin and receptor-mediated mitophagy, and how their disruption contributes to fibrotic tissue changes. The review also discusses potential therapeutic strategies that target mitophagy to treat or slow the disease.
papers.why: Although focused on lung disease, this review synthesizes core mitophagy molecular mechanisms that are directly transferable to understanding mitochondrial quality control in neurons.
